To underrate something means to judge it as less valuable, less important, or less capable than it truly is. When you underrate something, your opinion of it is lower than it deserves. You are giving it less credit than it has earned.
The simplest way to picture it

Think of every person, skill, or thing as having a "true rating" — a fair score reflecting how good or capable it actually is. When you underrate something, you assign it a score that is too low. Your mistake goes in one specific direction: downward, below the truth.

Here is a concrete image. A chef is genuinely extraordinary — a 9 out of 10 by any fair measure. But you have only seen him cook once, on a bad day, so you assume he is average — maybe a 5. You have underrated him. Your judgment fell below reality.

"Most people underrate how much hard work goes into painting."
People believe painting takes less effort than it really does. Their estimate of its difficulty is set too low.

"Don't underrate her — she is one of the best engineers in the company."
A warning not to dismiss someone whose true ability is high.

"He tends to underrate himself and never applies for jobs he is more than qualified for."
This is about underrating yourself — setting the measure of your own abilities below where they actually belong. This is one of the most common ways the word is used.

"That little restaurant is so underrated. The food is incredible, but almost nobody knows about it."
Here, "underrated" is used as a describing word (adjective) for something whose true quality goes unrecognized by the world.

The word is very flexible. You can underrate a person, a place, a skill, an idea, a subject, a risk, or even yourself. Any time something has a true worth and someone's opinion of it falls below that worth, "underrate" is the right word.
The most important thing to understand

"Underrate" always points in one specific direction — downward, below the truth. You are not making a random neutral mistake. You are specifically thinking too little of something. That directional nature is the heart of the word.

The direct opposite is overrate — to judge something as better, more capable, or more important than it actually is. "Many people overrate expensive skincare products — the cheaper ones work just as well."

So there are two ways to misjudge anything. Underrating means your opinion is too low. Overrating means your opinion is too high. A fair, accurate judgment is neither.
How it compares to similar words

Several words sit close to "underrate" in meaning, and knowing the differences will make your understanding much sharper.

Underestimate is about making a prediction or calculation that turns out to be too low — often about numbers, time, or someone's strength. "I underestimated how long the drive would take." The focus is on a guess or forecast being wrong, not on a rating of quality.

Undervalue means to place too low a worth on something, often in a financial or emotional sense. "The painting was undervalued at auction." It leans toward monetary or sentimental worth.

Underappreciate means to fail to feel or show enough gratitude or admiration for something. "He felt underappreciated despite all his hard work." It is more about emotional recognition and gratitude.

Underrate, by contrast, is specifically about the overall rating — the opinion or evaluation of someone's quality, ability, or importance being set too low. When you want to say "people do not think highly enough of this," underrate is the most fitting word.

In practice, "underrate" and "underestimate" overlap a great deal and are often interchangeable when talking about a person's ability. The differences above are subtle but real, and knowing them gives you a full picture.

When you call something "underrated," there is often a quietly protective, championing quality to it — you are the one who sees its true worth while others have missed it. "This is the most underrated book I have ever read" is almost a form of praise on behalf of something that has not gotten its due.

On the other hand, if you say "I underrated him," you are admitting a personal mistake — you misjudged someone, and now you know better. The word works equally well as both a defense of something and a confession of a poor judgment.
